summary.text: The difference of two squares is an identity that is one of the most commonly used in mathematics.
It can be pictured as the difference of two square areas in a plane.
Used in reverse, it removes square roots from denominators and gives complex fractions real denominators.

facts.label: Proof use
facts.value: It gives a simple proof of the AM–GM inequality in two variables

facts.label: Geometric picture
facts.value: The shaded gap between two square areas, a² − b²

facts.label: Complex numbers
facts.value: It finds linear factors of a sum of two squares

facts.label: Odd squares
facts.value: The difference of two odd perfect squares is a multiple of 8

facts.label: Galileo's law
facts.value: A falling object covers 3, 5, 7 times the first distance

paragraphs.heading: The identity
paragraphs.text: The difference of two squares is the identity a² − b² = (a + b) (a − b). It is one of the most widely used identities in all of mathematics. It also offers an easy proof of the AM–GM inequality for two variables, among many other uses.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is true
paragraphs.text: Multiply out (a + b) (a − b) with the distributive law and you get a² + b a − a b − b². By the commutative law, b a − a b = 0, so the middle terms cancel and a² − b² is left. This argument works for elements of any commutative ring, not just for numbers. Going the other way, if the identity holds for every pair of elements in a ring, that ring has to be commutative.

paragraphs.heading: Cutting and moving a square
paragraphs.text: Start with a large square of side a with a smaller square of side b removed, so the shaded region left has area a² − b². Cut that region into two rectangles: the top one is a wide and a − b tall, and the bottom one is a − b wide and b tall. Detach the smaller piece, turn it, and place it to the right of the larger one. Together they form a rectangle a + b wide and a − b tall, with area (a + b) (a − b). Moving pieces does not change the area, so a² − b² = (a + b) (a − b).

paragraphs.heading: An arithmetic shortcut
paragraphs.text: The identity also works as an arithmetic shortcut. When two numbers have an average that is easy to square, their product can be rewritten as a difference of two squares. For example, 27 × 33 is (30 − 3) times (30 + 3), which equals 30² − 3², or 891.

paragraphs.heading: Tidying up fractions
paragraphs.text: Run in reverse, the identity helps rationalise irrational denominators, a way of removing surds when dividing by certain combinations of square roots. For instance, the denominator 4 + √3 can be turned into 13. It also finds the linear factors of a sum of two squares once complex coefficients are allowed. Those two factors are complex conjugates, so the trick run backwards multiplies a complex number to get a real number, and that is how complex fractions get real denominators.

paragraphs.heading: Falling objects
paragraphs.text: Galileo's law of odd numbers grows out of the difference of consecutive squares. It says that if an object falling from rest, without resistance and in uniform gravity, covers some distance in one time interval, it covers 3, 5, 7 and so on times that distance in the following intervals of equal length. The reason is that the distance fallen is proportional to the square of the time, so at whole-number times the distances from the start are consecutive squares.

paragraphs.heading: Hunting for factors
paragraphs.text: Differences of squares also power several algorithms in number theory and cryptography that look for factors of whole numbers. A simple one is Fermat's factorization method, which looks for a number a where a² − N is a perfect square b². If it finds one, then N = (a + b) (a − b), which may split N into smaller factors. A more general form of this trick is the basis of several factoring algorithms, such as the quadratic sieve.
